IN RE: MARK F MILLER JR
PETITION FOR Review for Personal Income Tax
PERIOD(S) 2011
AND NOW, May 20, 2014, pursuant to the Fiscal Code, the Act of 1929, April 9, P.L. 343,
as amended, (72 P.S. § 1 et seq), the Board of Finance and Revenue of the Commonwealth of
Pennsylvania, based upon the reasons set forth herein, hereby ORDERS the following:
Jurisdiction
This petition comes before the Board of Finance and Revenue pursuant to Section 2704
of the Tax Reform Code, as amended, 72 P.S. § 9704.
Issue
Whether Petitioner has established that the Department improperly disallowed his
claimed Schedule UE expenses.
Statement of the Case
Petitioner, Mark F. Miller Jr., timely filed his 2011 Form PA-40, reporting $ of
gross compensation and deducting $ in Schedule UE expenses for a net compensation
of $ . Petitioner reported $ of taxable income and a tax liability of $ .
The Department reviewed the return and determined that Petitioner’s Schedule UE
expenses were excessive in relation to his compensation, and disallowed all claimed
expenses. The Department increased his tax liability to $ , and issued an assessment
notice for the additional tax due, plus penalties and interest.
Petitioner appealed the assessment notice to the Board of Appeals (“BOA”) on May 3,
2013, claiming that all of the expenses were correct as originally filed. In its Decision and
Order dated October 1, 2013, the BOA denied the petition, finding that the mileage and other
travel expenses should be classified as commuting miles, which are not deductible, and that

the meals and entertainment expenses claimed are not ordinary, reasonable, and actually
incurred in performing the duties of the job.
Petitioner files the instant matter at the Board of Finance and Revenue raising the same
claims as raised at the BOA. Petitioner avers he was an insurance sales representative and in
the course of his duties he was required to use his vehicle, cellphone, and incur other costs
that were not reimbursed by his employer. Petitioner states he was compensated through
commissions only, and the expenses incurred in his travel were reasonable and necessary in
order to earn such commissions. Petitioner also argues that it was customary in his profession
to provide periodic meals and entertainment for purposes of representing his products and
securing subsequent sales. Petitioner argues that while the Department may consider these
expenses to be excessive in comparison to his income, it should be noted that he was a recent
college graduate and was newly learning the intricacies of the position while incurring these
expenses.
Petitioner has submitted a letter from Northwestern Mutual Financial Network verifying
that he was a statutory employee responsible for any expenses incurred in the generation of
income.
In a letter mailed March 11, 2014, Board Counsel requested that Petitioner provide a
mileage log detailing the dates and locations traveled and the business purpose, along with
receipts, invoices, and other verification of the expenses claimed. As of this date, no further
evidence has been submitted.
Statement of the Law
An employee who is required, as a condition of her employment, to pay all her
expenses and who is not reimbursed separately for these expenses is permitted to exclude
from income the amount to be paid for legitimate business expenses. See Commonwealth v.
Staley, 476 Pa. 171, 381 A.2d 1280 (1978); Ritz v. Commonwealth, 495 Pa. 1, 432 A.2d 169
(1981).
Legitimate business expenses are those which are ordinary, actual, reasonable and
necessary to the business conducted. See Ritz 495 Pa. 1, 6, 432 A.2d 169 (1981).
Except as otherwise provided by this act, in all cases of petitions filed pursuant to this
article, the burden of proof shall be upon the petitioner or appellant, as the case may be.
72 P.S. § 9705.
Conclusion
Petitioner’s request for relief is denied. Legitimate business expenses are those which
are ordinary, actual, reasonable and necessary to the business conducted. See Ritz 495 Pa.
1, 6, 432 A.2d 169 (1981). While Petitioner has established that he was expected to incur
costs in the course of his employment for which he was not reimbursed, he has not provided
the requested evidence verifying those expenses. Petitioner has failed to meet his burden of
proof imposed by 72 P.S. § 9705.
